newsitem.title: USA: House-Senate Republicans agree on tax stance.
newsitem.headline: House-Senate Republicans agree on tax stance.

text.p: House and Senate Republicans agreed Tuesday to a stance on tax legislation from which they will bargain with the White House that included items opposed by President Clinton.

"Republicans are ready sometime tomorrow ... to start discussing the issues with the White House. We have reached sufficient agreement among ourselves," Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said.

Republicans will discuss with White House officials their plan for a net $85 billion tax cut over five years aimed at fulfilling the tax portion of the May balanced-budget agreement between congressional leaders and Clinton.
The Republican plan will include a reduction in the maximum capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from the current 28 percent.

The proposal will also include "indexing" which lowers the taxable amount of profits on investments such as stocks by taking into account the effect of inflation. The White House opposes that provision due to a concern it could produce higher budget deficits in later years.

The capital gains "indexing" provision would be allowed for assets held more than five years, a modification from the House bill which would have allowed it for assets held more than three years, Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said.

"We do still have indexing in there. We think we should not be paying taxes on inflation," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said. "We know the administration has heartburn about that."
Tax committee staffers were to add up all the provisions of the new united Republican tax plan to determine the amount of the tax cut.
That figure will determine whether a cigarette tax increase will be included in the Republican tax proposal, a congressional aide said.
The Senate bill includes a 20-cents per pack cigarette tax increase to raise about $15 billion over five years, with about half going to pay for childrens' health programmes.

But House Republicans have said there was little support for that tax increase on their side. House tax negotiators "agreed in principle" to a tobacco tax increase if it is needed to make the total package amount to an $85 billion net tax cut, and that would also determine the amount of any cigarette tax increase, the aide said.

Another issue still undecided was the difference in House and Senate bills about extending the ethanol subsidy which expires at the end of 2000. Ethanol is a supplement to gasoline made from domestic corn.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, is vehemently opposed to extending the subsidy, while some Senate Republicans are fighting to keep it after it expires at perhaps reduced levels.
"We had a very, very good negotiation," House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, said after the House-Senate Republican tax meeting. "We're very close to getting this done," he added.

On another hot-button issue, Republicans will present to White House officials a proposal that would allow fewer low-income working families to receive the $500 per child tax credit than the administration wants.
Republicans say the $500 per child tax credit should go to families who pay income taxes.
